course.title: Use a Hand Knitting Pattern with Your Knitting Machine

components.html:
The goals of this course:
  1. Use a HK pattern as inspiration and convert the written instructions to MK instructions
  2. Use the converted pattern and substitute yarn (change the gauge)
  3. Use a HK pattern as inspiration,use a Knit it Now Dynamic pattern for a larger size range and incorporate the designer details.

components.title: How do you go about using a hand knitting pattern with your knitting machine?

components.html:
Big Hug is a simple pattern by Josée Paquin. http://www.uandiknit.com/this website is no longer active
The pattern is available on Ravelry. Josée has generously allowed us to use her pattern to work with for this course.
The pattern has been very popular for it's simplicity and updated styling.
The design can be easily "translated" to machine knitting.
Follow along as we analyze this pattern.
The steps used can be applied to ANY hand knitting pattern.

blocks.title: Knit a HK pattern on the Knitting Machine

components.html:
The first step is to determine the gauge in the original pattern.
Do the math and establish the gauge in 1" or 1cm.
4" / 10 cm 1 inch 1 cm
13 sts 3.25 sts 1.3 sts
18 rows 4.5 rows 1.8 rows
Why determine gauge in 1 inch / 1 cm?
One of the biggest differences between HK and MK patterns is that hand knitting instructions are generally written in cm/inches, but we need to know how many rows to knit. For example:
The instruction "Knit 9 cm / 3.5 inches" doesn't work for machine knitters (no guessing allowed). We need to know how many rows to knit.
Using the information we calculated above:
Pattern Instructions: Knit 9 cm / 3.5 inches
Machine Knitting Instructions: Knit [9cm x 1.8=16 rows] [3.5" x 4.5 =16] rows
Practice "Translating"

components.html:
GAUGE SWATCH for matching gauge

I recently had an epiphany about swatching when I'm trying to MATCH gauge.  In the past I've knit my gauge swatches as I learned as a machine knitter.   I never use the gauge rulers that came with my machines, but I've always knit my swatches according to the "rules". (DUH) On my standard machine, I've dutifully cast on 60 stitches and knit 60 rows between marked rows .  I marked off 40 stitches and got out my regular ruler, measured and did the math. Being a total non-math person, I can't tell you how many times I've messed up the calculation of my gauge ... even when using a calculator.

THE EPIPHANY: I was hand knitting a HK pattern.  Hand knitting the complicated sections of the pattern was fun, but I decided that knitting a whole lot of stockinette (the boring stuff by hand) was dumb.  So I threaded up my machine and started to knit a swatch.
The gauge I needed to match was 24 sts and 30 rows per 4".
  •  I cast 60 stitches (so I could easily measure 24 stitches)
  •  I knit a few rows with my main yarn (marking with eyelets the tension gauge)
  •  2 rows of a contrasting color
  •  Knit 30 rows
  •  2 rows of a contrasting color
  •  A few main yarn rows and bound off
  • AT THE SAME TIME I also marked  the stitches that were framing my desired 24 stitches.
In other words, instead of marking the traditional number of stitches and rows, I broke the "rules" and marked my DESIRED GAUGE  of 24 stitches and 30 rows as I knit the swatch.
I let the swatch rest, then wet blocked it and let it sit overnight. The next day, I put my handy-dandy 4" measuring tool down on my swatch.  (see below about my DIY 4" tool) As you can see, by the first photo, my stitch gauge was good, but my row gauge needed to be adjusted.  It was easy to see through my tool that I had too many rows to 4".   I adjusted my mast tension, knit another swatch and VOILA!  I was able to match my gauge EXACTLY --- with NO MATH!
Stitch Gauge is close - but the row gauge is off

24 sts x 30 rows = 4" ! Success!
 

Template

For my tool, I cut a 4" x 4" square of quilters template plastic (readily available at craft stores) to create my Handy-dandy tool. Because it's see-through, I can see my marked stitches and rows on my swatch.
You could use a square of any material (cardboard, paper, clear plastic of any kind).
We've created a to-scale template for you to print. Print the template on paper, a transparency or card stock and try it. You will be amazed at how much easier it is to measure gauge (for both hand and machine knitting).

Because this pattern doesn't have a diagram, we'll need to create our own.
This is the basic shape of the sweater - it's long-sleeved, drop shoulder with a small funnel neck collar.
Next we will start filling in the blanks based on the written pattern.

lessons.title: Convert the Pattern to Another Gauge

components.html:
The yarn that was originally used for the Big Hug has been discontinued. Chances are you won't be able to match the designer's gauge.
Grab a calculator and use the Gauge Conversion Tool to successfully knit the sweater with your choice of yarn.
Remember: Swatching is NOT optional. You MUST have measured your swatch ACCURATELY for success.

For this exercise, use the stitches and rows we previously established for the body of our Big Hug
.
Pattern gauge: 13sts/18rows = 4"/10cm
New Gauge: 28sts/44rows = 4"/10cm
  1. Use the tool below to establish the multiplier for the new gauge
      Enter the Pattern gauge and the New Gauge below
  2. Record the multiplier for stitch and row
  3. Multiple each section by the correct ratio
  4. Scroll down to enter your answers (and check your math)

Tip: Convert all the stitches at one time, then all the rows at one time

After converting the gauge of a pattern using the Gauge Conversion Tool, you will no longer be able to follow the original knitting pattern shaping instructions.
Knit it Now offers 3 tools for the most common shaping situations:
  1. Magic Formula Tools(example: shaped sleeves)
  2. Slope Tool (example: Shoulder shaping)
  3. Neckline tool(re-calculate round necklines)
For more complicated shaping or for creating your own designs, we suggest studying knitting pattern drafting books. There are many available in libraries and online. The investment in time to learn pattern drafting will be invaluable to you on your knitting journey.

Recommended Reading
The Knitters guide to Sweater Design - Carmen Michelson / Mary - Ann Davis.
This book is out of print, but you can find copies online. It was published by Interweave press and presents all the math and formulas you will ever need in a clear and easy-to-understand manner.
Knitwear Design Workshop
This book is still in print and readily available from Amazon. Purchase using this link and Knit it Now receives a small commission.

You may not want to chart knitting patterns from start to finish, but if you substitute yarns and change gauge in a pattern, you'll need to re-chart shaping for your pattern.
The Knit it Now Tools are designed to give you a hand with the math. Easy-to-use and accurate, these tools will go a long way to knitting garments that fit!
To accurately re-calculate shoulder shaping, use the Knit it Now Slope Tool

The Magic Formula (AKA the Diophantine Equation) is used to calculate even increases and decreases for knitting.
If you shorten or lengthen a shaped piece or you convert the gauge, these tools are invaluable for keeping the guess work out of increase and decrease placement.
No Math! Try the tools!

components.title: 3 Ways to Incorporate Hand Knitting Patterns in your Machine Knitting World

components.html:
Designer Ellen Kindsvater ran with the idea of a simple Funnel neck pullover. Here are her designer elements to the basic design.
A few minor changes to Big Hug, knit on the standard gauge machine with a textured stitch pattern and WOW! A completely different look from the same pattern.
  • G-Carriage Stitch pattern (see below)
  • She simplified the shape sleeve for less shaping with the g-carriage
  • 3/4" funnel for less bulk
  • No ribbing
  • Back is 2" longer than the front
  • Side slit - 4" in front and 6" in back
Ellen shared some finishing techniques:
  • To ensure the neck is stretchy enough to go over the head, she worked a loose "around the gatepeg" bind off.
  • She used the same bind off edges for the top of the sleeves so they wouldn't be too tight in the armhole.
  • To prevent flair at the hem, she cast on with waste yarn and ravel cord. When the knitting was complete, she rehung the cast on edges and bound off tightly not around the gate peg).
  • After dressing her swatch Ellen discovered that the ribbed stitch pattern she used caused the knitting to relax and become wider and shorter.
  • With the knit and purl stitch pattern she chose, either side can be the public (right) side
